The first run was fast, the second run had a slower prompt evaluation, the third run generated faster, and none of them throttled, but I also changed the context shape between runs and I am trying to understand which variable actually mattered.

I have three different symptoms at once: recall is finding the right memory, the model answer is still slightly wrong, and the TTS starts later than before, so consider all three parts together instead of treating this as one isolated bug.

I spent a while testing this because the service starts correctly, the model is warm, the prefix hash matches, and the router only takes about a millisecond, yet one path is still much slower, and I want an explanation that accounts for all of those facts.

Here is the whole situation: the Pi is headless, PipeWire is working, the USB audio device is selected, the model is already loaded, and the first token still varies by more than a second depending on the prompt shape, so help me reason through the architecture.

I tried the old configuration, then the new configuration, then rolled back only the thread count while leaving the context changes in place, and the result improved only halfway, which makes me think two things are interacting rather than one setting being solely responsible.

The code passes the unit tests, but the live voice test behaves differently because Whisper sometimes changes short words, the router sees raw text now, and memory lookup adds context on some routes, so I want you to analyze how those pieces could combine.

My concern is not just this one misroute. The classifier is fast enough, the regex rules are hard to maintain, the tests started depending on the rules, and every new wording adds another edge case, so explain the architectural implications of removing the regex layer.

There are several observations I want you to keep together: the model file is small, prediction is around one millisecond, word ngrams capture phrases, character ngrams help spelling variation, and logistic regression gives us probabilities, so explain why that stack fits this router.

I want the long version here because I am comparing two designs, one where the harness decides intent with hand written rules and another where a trained classifier decides intent, and I care about latency, maintainability, generalization, and failure modes.

I tested greetings, farewells, memory recall, directives, and detailed prompts, and most of them work, but tiny replies like yup and nope are less reliable while long questions are strong, so explain what that pattern says about the training distribution.

The install worked, audio works, the LLM is warm, and the router is fast, but I still want to understand why the semantic classifier can replace a lot of brittle Python without replacing deterministic memory extraction after the route is chosen.
